title: Question 7

parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 7.1 as a single closed loop with no battery or supply after the switch closes - think about where the p.d. to drive current through R must come from.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply Kirchhoff Around the Single Loop**
Think of the charged capacitor as a temporary battery. Once the switch is closed there is only $C$ and $R$ in one loop, so going round the loop the sum of p.d.s must be zero. That means all the p.d. across the capacitor appears across the resistor at every instant: $$V_C - V_R = 0$$ so $$V_C = V_R$$

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Fig. 7.2 is a straight line through the origin of $Q$ against $V_C$ - recall what physical quantity links charge stored to p.d. across a capacitor.
Hint 2: Pick a clear point on the line, for example at $V_C = 12\text{ V}$, read off $Q$ in $\text{mC}$ and remember to convert $\text{mC}$ to $\text{C}$ before dividing.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Gradient to Capacitance**
For any capacitor, charge and p.d. are directly proportional: $$Q = C V_C$$ So $C = Q / V_C$ and the gradient of the $Q$ against $V_C$ graph in Fig. 7.2 is $C$.

Step 2: **Read Values and Calculate**
At the start of discharge $V_C = 12\text{ V}$ and from Fig. 7.2: $$Q_0 = 7.2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ C}$$ Then: $$C = \frac{Q_0}{V_C} = \frac{7.2 \times 10^{-3}}{12} = 6.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ F}$$ Convert to microfarad: $$C = 6.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{6} = 600\text{ }\mu\text{F}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Fig. 7.3 is a straight line of $I$ against $V_R$ for the resistor - think about which law links current through a resistor to p.d. across it.
Hint 2: Choose an easy point such as $V_R = 8.0\text{ V}$ where $I = 1.0\text{ mA}$, convert $\text{mA}$ to $\text{A}$, then rearrange for $R$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Ohm's Law for the Resistor**
The resistor obeys: $$V_R = I R$$ So: $$R = \frac{V_R}{I}$$ The gradient of $I$ against $V_R$ is $1/R$.

Step 2: **Read Values and Calculate**
From Fig. 7.3, when $V_R = 8.0\text{ V}$: $$I = 1.0\text{ mA} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A}$$ Then: $$R = \frac{8.0}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 8000\text{ }\Omega = 8.0\text{ k}\Omega$$ Any other point on the line gives the same result because it is linear.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: the time constant $\tau$ of the circuit.
hints: Hint 1: The speed of a capacitor discharge is set by both how much charge must flow and how hard it is to push that charge - recall how $R$ and $C$ combine to give the time constant.
Hint 2: Use your values of $R$ in ohms and $C$ in farads (not kΩ and μF) so the product comes out in seconds.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the Time Constant**
For a capacitor-resistor circuit the characteristic time is: $$\tau = R C$$ It is the time for $Q$, $V$ and $I$ to fall to $1/e$ of the initial value.

Step 2: **Substitute in SI Units**
Use $R = 8000\text{ }\Omega$ and $C = 6.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ F}$: $$\tau = 8000 \times 6.0 \times 10^{-4} = 4.8\text{ s}$$

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Use Fig. 7.2, Fig. 7.3 and your answer in (a) to explain why the variation of $Q$ with $t$ is exponential in nature.

markscheme_points.text: Any two points from: • charge and current are both (directly) proportional to voltage • charge is (directly) proportional to current • current is the rate of change of charge
Q is proportional to the rate of change of Q (so exponential variation)

hints: Hint 1: Look at the shapes of Fig. 7.2 and Fig. 7.3 - both are straight lines through the origin, so what does that tell you about how $Q$ depends on $V_C$ and how $I$ depends on $V_R$?
Hint 2: Now combine those ideas with your answer in (a) where $V_C = V_R$ - if both $Q$ and $I$ are proportional to the same voltage, how are $Q$ and $I$ related to each other?

Hint 3: Remember the definition of current in terms of charge flow during discharge, $I = -dQ/dt$ - what kind of decay do you get when the rate of loss of a quantity is proportional to the quantity itself?
parts.proper_answer: From Fig. 7.2 $Q$ is directly proportional to $V_C$ and from Fig. 7.3 $I$ is directly proportional to $V_R$. Since $V_C = V_R$, $Q$ is directly proportional to $I$. But $I$ is the rate of decrease of $Q$, so rate of change of $Q$ is proportional to $Q$, which gives exponential variation of $Q$ with $t$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read Proportionality From the Two Graphs**
Fig. 7.2 is $Q$ against $V_C$ through the origin, so: $$Q \propto V_C$$ Fig. 7.3 is $I$ against $V_R$ through the origin, so: $$I \propto V_R$$ This is just $Q = CV_C$ and $V_R = IR$ in graphical form.

Step 2: **Link Q Directly to I**
From (a) $V_C = V_R$ at all times during the discharge. So both $Q$ and $I$ are proportional to the same changing voltage. Eliminate $V$: $$Q = C V \text{ and } I = V/R$$ giving $$Q \propto I$$ In words, the charge left is proportional to the discharge current flowing.

Step 3: **Spot the Exponential Condition**
Current is the rate of flow of charge off the plates. For discharge: $$I = -\frac{dQ}{dt}$$ So the rate at which $Q$ decreases is proportional to $Q$ itself: $$\frac{dQ}{dt} \propto -Q$$ Whenever rate of change is proportional to the amount present, the solution is exponential: $$Q = Q_0 e^{-t/RC}$$ That is why $Q$ against $t$ is exponential in nature.
